seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p:
Dear Pound: Sorry to hear you have been laid up. I was too, which is one reason for the delay in writing. Everybody here is ill with a tiresome form of influenza. Tomorrow I shall forward you a letter for Quinn so that you may read it and redirect it simply. Meanwhile I shall try to cable him in Lieber’s or ABC code if I can find a copy of one. Have you a spare copy of The Dial with Miss Scott’s article about Ulysses
? It is not on sale in Paris, is it? As regards the trial in New York the person, I think, who enjoyed it most, between his judicial chambers and the courtroom, was Magistrate Corrigan. I hope he had a supply of moonshine concealed in his umbrella handle to complete his bliss.

News from here. Of Mr Fels no trace. People are still writing, wiring, telephoning to Mr Valette Vallette
about me and he is trying to find out who, what and where I am. Mr Fontainas is still reading the frontispiece of A.P.O.T.A.A.A.Y.M. and Mrs Bloch does not seem to have done much of the translation. She is not in good health, I think, or has worries of some kind so I don’t press her about it all the more as it would not mean publication. Mr Budry, editor of Ecrits Nouveaux , was enthusiastic about publishing it in his review but having measured it with a footrule he finds it too long. He then proposed to translate Ulysses which he has not read. One evening he ran after me through the Cimmerian obscurity of
la ville lumière
and begged me to allow him to translate Dubliners . I gave him permission. A Miss Pointet , a friend of his, translated A Mother (a story in Dubliners) and submitted it to me asking to be put right on certain points. The translation was very faulty so I wrote asking her to call so that we might go over it together. No answer. I met Mr Budry by chance a few days ago. He told me he had written to Mrs Bloch twice about sending it (the translation) in for publication by Emile Paul, their reader Mr Suarès being an admirer of the book. He got no answer from her. Mrs Bloch told me that she did not answer because he is not serious.

As regards Exiles a mot-à-mot of the play was made by a person named
Nathanson Natanson
who, Miss Serruys says, is a hack secretary of Lugne Poe’s. The translation she found very bad. I didn’t read it. Lugne Poe now sends a message to the effect that he will produce Exiles if I give in writing what he calls carte blanche to Mr Nathanson Natanson to adapt the play as he may think fit.

It was a presentiment of these things coupled with material troubles which, during the two occasions when I was admitted to the society of artistic, literary and political celebrities here, caused a thoughtful expression to steal gradually over my handsome features.

Would you believe this? Yesterday I received a letter from the governing council of the commercial university of Trieste , as they call it, stating that some supplementary examinations have to be held and offering me an examiner’s fee of one lira (2½ d) per candidate! I am having copies of the letter made, and will send you one.

div.note: The Russian-born Ludmila Bloch-Savitsky (1881-1957) and her husband, a railroad chief engineer named Marcel Bloch (1881-1951), had allowed JJ and family to live in their Paris flat at 5 rue de l’Assomption, rent-free, for their first three months in Paris. The Blochs wanted the flat back at the end of October 1920 (LI 148). JJ wrote Pound on 5 November 1920 that after an “entire month of flathunting,” he and his family were back at 9 rue de l’Université, the private hotel with furnished rooms they had stayed at when they first arrived in Paris in July 1920 (LIII 27). They remained there until the beginning of December 1920.

Pound wrote John Quinn on 8 November 1920: “Am typing this [in] bed (fog, throat etc.) … Expect to be out in a day or two” (The Selected Letters of Ezra Pound to John Quinn, 1915-1924, ed. Timothy Materer [Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 1991], 201).

JJ wrote John Quinn on 17 November 1920 that in early November he was “ill with a kind of influenza” (Myron Schwartzman, “‘Quinnigan’s Quake!’ John Quinn’s Letters to James Joyce, 1916-1920,” Bulletin of Research in the Humanities, vol. 81, no. 2 [Summer 1978]: 254).
The deadly influenza pandemic known as the Spanish flu lasted from early 1918 until spring 1920. Rashes of flu, typically less deadly, continued to break out afterwards.

JJ wrote the New York lawyer John Quinn (1870-1924) on 17 November 1920 (John Quinn Memorial Collection, Manuscripts & Archives Division, New York Public Library), repeating points he had made in his letter to Pound of 5 November 1920, including his fear that his American publisher B.W. Huebsch (1876-1964) might try to pirate Ulysses as a book (see JJ to Pound, 5 November 1920; LIII 27-28). JJ asks Pound here simply to “redirect” to Quinn his present letter, because Pound exploded with irritation when JJ earlier asked him to make for Quinn a “digest” of his 5 November letter to Pound. “Where you think I am to get time to ‘brief’ yr. epistle – I dont know,” Pound wrote JJ in a letter also dated (oddly) 5 November 1920 (Robert Spoo, “Unpublished Letters of Ezra Pound to James, Nora, and Stanislaus Joyce,” James Joyce Quarterly, vol. 32, no. 3-4 [Spring-Summer 1995]: 539).

Various codes had been developed to disguise and abbreviate telegram messages. Benjamin Franklin Lieber (1853-1915) published a popular code in Lieber’s Standard Telegraphic Code (New York: Lieber Publishing Co., 1896). William Clauson-Thue (1834-1907) created a hugely successful code, known as the ABC Code, that was described in The ABC Universal Commercial Electric Telegraphic Code (London, 1873). In cabling Quinn, JJ used what he called “Scott’s Code, American edition” (LIII 30), possibly some version of E.B. Scott’s The Ship Owners’ Telegraphic Code, 2nd ed. (London, 1880).

The American novelist and poet Evelyn Scott (1893-1963) published an article, “A Contemporary of the Future,” in The Dial, vol. 69 (October 1920): 353-67, ranging over all of JJ’s published works and concluding with praise for Ulysses: “James Joyce, to my mind, expresses, more clearly than any other writer of English prose in this time, the conviction of modernity – a new and complex knowledge of self which has passed its period of racial gestation and is ready for birth in art” (367). Pound thought that Scott’s essay was an example of the stodginess he was trying to expel from The Dial. “All right to boost Joyce,” he wrote John Quinn on 9 October 1920, “but a fifteen page pompous female essay in a number that has nothing, practically but essays…!!!!” (Selected Letters of Ezra Pound to John Quinn, 196).

On 21 October 1920, the New York lawyer John Quinn (1870-1924) appeared at the Jefferson Market Police Court in New York to defend his clients, the Little Review editors Margaret Caroline Anderson (1886-1973) and Jane Heap (1883-1964), against charges of having published an obscene issue containing the portion of the “Nausicaa” episode of Ulysses in which Leopold Bloom masturbates at the seashore. Magistrate Judge Joseph Eugene Corrigan (1875-1935), who presided at this preliminary hearing, repaired to his judicial chambers at one point to read the contested passages. Quinn reported all this to Pound on 21 October 1920 (in the language JJ alludes to here): “I don’t know whether the judicial urinal or judicial water closet abutted on his chambers but I supposed it did. At any rate, chambers struck me as the right place for him to read the July-August number.” After arguments by counsel, Judge Corrigan ruled that the passage “where the man went off in his pants [was] smutty, filthy within the meaning of the statute.” At the end of the hearing, Judge Corrigan bound the defendants over for trial in the Court of Special Sessions (quoted in Paul Vanderham, James Joyce and Censorship: The Trials of Ulysses [London: Macmillan, 1998], 44, 46; for a more complete account of the case, see JJ to Pound, 5 November 1920, notes; LIII 27-28).

Florent Fels (1891–1977), French publisher, journalist, and author, had planned to issue a French translation of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man in his journal, Action: Cahiers de philosophie et d’art (LI 120; The Cornell Joyce Collection, 69-70). Candidates for translator were, first, Louis Bagnan (LII 450), then Ludmila Bloch-Savitzky (LI 142), but Fels produced only a review of the novel in Action, no. 6 (December 1920): 63–64. The translation by Savitzky (1881-1957) was published as a book, Dedalus; Portrait de l’artiste jeune par lui-même, by the Paris house, Éditions de La Sirène, in 1924.

JJ had hopes – unrealized in the end – that a French translation of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man would be published serially in the journal Mercure de France, founded and edited by Alfred Vallette (1858-1935). For more details, see JJ to Pound, 28 September 1920, notes.

André Fontainas (1865-1948), Belgian poet, novelist, critic, art historian, and good friend of Ludmila Bloch-Savitzky (1881-1957). Both were trying – fruitlessly, as it turned out – to persuade the journal Mercure de France to serialize a French translation of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (see JJ to Pound, 28 September 1920, notes).

Paul Budry (1883-1949), Swiss writer and art critic who founded, with André Germain, the journal Les Écrits nouveaux in 1917. This review did not publish a French translation of A Portrait. It did, however, publish French translations of JJ’s stories, “Eveline” and “Araby,” by Hélène du Pasquier, and “A Little Cloud,” by Yva Fernandez, in November 1921, February 1922, and December 1922, respectively (for details, see John J. Slocum and Herbert Cahoon, A Bibliography of James Joyce [New Haven: Yale University Press, 1953], 112-13).

note.p: In a manner typical of his two-plane thinking while writing Ulysses, JJ here combines the Cimmerian land of darkness, mentioned in Book 11 of The Odyssey, and the modern-day Paris, City of Light (la ville lumière). Homer’s passage describing the Cimmerian land comes just after Odysseus and his men have left the island of the sorceress Circe, whose ability to transform men into beasts forms the general theme of “Circe,” the fifteenth episode of Ulysses, on which JJ was laboring at this time. Pound translated the relevant portion of The Odyssey in his Canto 1:

lg.l: Came we then to the bounds of deepest water,
To the Kimmerian lands, and peopled cities
Covered with close-webbed mist, unpierced ever
Nor with stars stretched, nor looking back from heaven
Swartest night stretched over wretched men there.

div.note: Uncertain. A “Mlle Pointet” was a member of the Société Française de Musicologie and attended meetings of the Société at the Salle Gaveau, the classical concert hall in Paris, in 1921 (“Comptes Rendus des Séances de la Société,” Bulletin de la Société française de musicologie, vol. 2, no. 9 (July 1921): 157-161). There is no particular reason to believe that this Mademoiselle Pointet was JJ’s “Miss Pointet,” except that the latter chose to translate the most musical of the Dubliners stories and, according to JJ, did so rather inexpertly, perhaps because her interest and skill were more musical than literary. We offer this possibility as a direction for research.

“A Mother,” the thirteenth story in JJ’s Dubliners (1914), was tenth in the order of composition, completed by late September 1905. Based on JJ’s early experience of Dublin musical circles, the story depicts the grim, uncompromising determination of Mrs. Kearney to advance her daughter Kathleen, a pianist, in the social and cultural ranks of the Irish Revival. Mrs. Kearney brokers a contract for her daughter to perform at a series of concerts, but on the final evening she refuses to allow Kathleen to take the stage after the interval until she has been paid the full amount of the contract. When the organizers are unable to produce the entire sum on the spot, Mrs. Kearney makes a scene and takes her daughter home, condemned by the entire company. The story satirizes the pretensions of the Irish Revival and explores the norms and expectations of musical performers and organizers in turn-of-the-century Dublin. The story has been the subject of important feminist readings (see, e.g., Margot Norris, Suspicious Readings of Joyce’s Dubliners [Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2003], 185-96).

The Paris publishing house Émile-Paul Frères, tracing its origins back to 1882, published, in addition to the journal Les Écrits nouveaux (1917-1922), works by the French poet and critic André Suarès (1868-1848), as well as works by Natalie Clifford Barney, Jean Giraudoux, Paul Valéry, and many other writers. In late October 1920, JJ appealed to Suarès for help in finding a new apartment, evidently without success (LIII 24).

Jacques Natanson (1901-1975) served as secretary to the French theater director Lugné-Poë at this time, but very soon was authoring his own plays, such as L’Age heureux (1922) and L’Enfant truqué (1922), both of which Lugné-Poë produced at Théâtre de l’Œuvre in Paris. Natanson was chosen to provide a French translation and adaptation of JJ’s Exiles, and the play was to be produced by Lugné-Poë (LIII 26, 36; Ellmann, JJ 498). But the project was abruptly called off by Lugné-Poë in June 1921 (for more details, see JJ to Pound, 18 August 1920, notes).

Jenny Serruys (1886-1983), a French literary figure who helped JJ and his family shortly after they arrived in Paris. She produced a French translation of Exiles (Les Exilés) which was published under her married name J.S. Bradley by nrf Gallimard in Paris in 1950 (for more details, see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1920, notes).

Aurélien-Marie Lugné (1869-1940), known as Lugné-Poë, was a French actor, theater director, and scenic designer who considered producing JJ’s play Exiles in Paris, but in June 1921 concluded that the effort would lose money (Ellmann, JJ 497-98; for a fuller account, see JJ to Pound, 18 August 1920, notes). For the “mot-à-mot” (word-for-word) translation of Exiles that Lugné-Poë used in working with the play (at least according to JJ), see JJ to Pound, 28 September 1920, notes.
JJ later told Harriet Shaw Weaver that “a cursory inspection” of Lugné-Poë had led him to suspect that he would not in the end produce Exiles (LI 166).

JJ’s phrasing here is reminiscent of popular novelistic prose of the nineteenth century: “A smile, a wicked smile of superiority, if not of contempt, stole over his handsome features” ([Anonymous], The Fair Carew; or, Husbands and Wives, vol. 1 [London: Smith, Elder, 1851], 65). This palpitating style remains a staple of romantic fiction to this day: “One moment he was wearing that remote, polite expression, then next, a genuine smile stole over his handsome features. She stared at it, her pulse shivering” (RaeAnne Thayne, Reunion on Rocky Shores [Harlequin Digital Sales Corp., 2020], n.p.). JJ ‘s most famous pastiche of this style is the “Nausicaa” episode of Ulysses, written, he said, in “a namby-pamby jammy marmalady drawersy (alto là!) style with effects of incense, mariolatry, masturbation, stewed cockles, painter’s palette, chitchat, circumlocutions, etc. etc.” (LI 135).

Both before and after the war, JJ taught the English language at the Scuola Superiore di Commercio Revoltella, a commercial high school in Trieste. After the postwar annexation of Trieste by Italy, with the issuance of a royal decree of 7 November 1920 (no. 1667), the school was granted the status of a university, equal to other such Italian institutions. But JJ preferred to call it “the revolver university” (LIII 10); it had been founded in 1877 by a bequest of Baron Pasquale Revoltella (1795-1869).
Twopence halfpenny in 1920 was worth about 50p in today’s money. Joyce’s usage is figurative rather than hyperbolic as “twopenny halfpenny” was also an epithet of disparagement (OED).
